lesson.title: Learned to React: The Conditioned Response
lesson.summary: A conditioned response is the learned reaction an organism produces to a conditioned stimulus, built on the same underlying reflex as the unconditioned response but now triggered by a stimulus that once meant nothing.
lesson.body:
The conditioned response is the payoff of the whole classical conditioning process: the reaction that a conditioned stimulus produces once learning has taken place. In Pavlov's dogs, salivation to the bell alone, with no food present, is the conditioned response. It is worth noticing that the conditioned response is usually the same basic type of reaction as the unconditioned response, salivation in both cases, but it is not always identical in strength; the learned version is often somewhat weaker or less consistent than the original automatic reflex.

One of the most famous, and most ethically troubling by modern standards, demonstrations of a conditioned response came from John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's early twentieth century study with an infant researchers referred to as Little Albert. The infant initially showed no fear of a white rat. The researchers then repeatedly paired the rat, which became the conditioned stimulus, with a loud, frightening noise, the unconditioned stimulus, which naturally produced a startle and distress reaction, the unconditioned response. After repeated pairings, the infant began to show a fear reaction, the conditioned response, to the rat by itself. The study is widely cited as an early demonstration that even emotional reactions like fear can be classically conditioned, though it is also a well known example of research that would not meet today's ethical standards, since a young child was deliberately conditioned to feel afraid with no clear record of the fear ever being reversed. Some historical details about what happened to the child afterward have been debated by historians and are not fully settled, so they are worth treating with caution rather than certainty.

Taken together, these four chapters trace one continuous process. An unconditioned stimulus produces an unconditioned response automatically. Pairing a neutral stimulus with that unconditioned stimulus turns it into a conditioned stimulus. And once that learning has occurred, the conditioned stimulus produces a conditioned response on its own, completing the shift from an automatic, built in reflex to a learned, associative one.
